teaser.text: Danaher sells the tools and supplies that help customers discover medicines, manufacture them, and diagnose patients. Its dollar comes in through instruments, materials, services, and repeat supplies, then goes out through production, research, selling, delivery, and support.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Danaher?

paragraphs.text: The bear case gives $4,100 million, $4,200 million, and $4,400 million because shipment delays, China pricing pressure, weaker research spending, and Masimo-related interest costs restrain margins. The bull case gives $4,900 million, $5,800 million, and $6,800 million because orders convert quickly, utilization improves, Masimo contributes, and debt falls. The base probability is highest because earnings stabilized after the pandemic-driven decline, but 2025 core growth missed its roughly 3% forecast.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Danaher really make?

paragraphs.text: Danaher’s own free-cash-flow measure was $5,293 million because it included proceeds from selling property and equipment. Deducting $298 million of stock compensation produces an analytical “real free cash flow” figure of $4,962 million, or 20.2% of revenue. Stock compensation is not a cash payment, but it can dilute owners or require repurchases. Cash is strong; the specialist still asks whether it remains strong after normal inventory needs, investment and dilution.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Danaher today?

paragraphs.text: The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, tells us how much investors pay for each dollar of profit. Danaher’s trailing P/E is 39.8x. Reported and adjusted earnings differ because acquisitions create intangible assets, such as customer relationships and technology, whose recorded cost is amortized over time. In the second quarter of 2026, reported EPS was $1.23, while adjusted EPS was $1.94. Adjusted earnings may clarify ongoing operations, but they also remove costs created by Danaher’s acquisition strategy.

Free cash flow is cash left after operations and necessary capital spending. Danaher generated about $5.1 billion in 2023 and $5.3 billion in 2025, but timing can distort one year’s result: selling inventory without replacing it can release cash without proving stronger demand. The 3.4% free-cash-flow yield therefore needs to be judged against the 5.21% ten-year Treasury yield and against debt repayment, reinvestment, acquisitions and dividends. The 0.7% dividend yield is only the portion paid directly to shareholders.

blocks.heading: How much does Danaher pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: The dividend starts from the latest $0.40 quarterly rate, or $1.60 annualized. The base case raises it by $0.12 annually to $1.72, $1.84, and $1.96, close to the company’s record of annual increases but moderated for higher debt. The bear case holds $1.60 throughout; the bull case reaches $1.80, $2.00, and $2.20 as stronger cash generation funds faster growth. Positive free cash flow supports no cut, but debt makes a pause credible.

blocks.heading: Is Danaher’s dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: After $1,156 million of capital spending, free cash flow was $5,260 million in 2025. That was nearly unchanged from $5,296 million in the prior year because capital spending fell from $1,392 million. Danaher does not disclose how much capital spending merely maintains the business and how much expands it.

paragraphs.text: Management expects earnings to recover more reliably than sales. Danaher’s July guidance calls for 2026 core sales growth of 3.0%–4.0% and adjusted earnings per share of $8.45–$8.60. Core sales remove acquisitions and currency movements, while adjusted earnings remove selected costs. These measures show operating progress, but they do not replace reported results.

blocks.heading: Did Danaher keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Danaher’s forecasts provide an accountability test. In July 2025, it forecast about 3% core revenue growth and adjusted EPS of US$7.70–US$7.80. It delivered the top of the EPS range but only 2% core growth. Core growth removes acquisition and currency effects, so earnings met the target while underlying growth missed. In July 2026, Masimo helped raise EPS guidance while core growth remained a separate concern.

blocks.heading: What has Danaher’s revenue and profit trend been?

paragraphs.text: June revenue reached $6,265 million, up from $5,936 million a year earlier. Reported growth was about 5.5%. Core growth was 3.0%, rising to 4.5% without respiratory testing. Life Sciences led at 5.5%; Biotechnology grew 2.5%, while Diagnostics grew 2.0%. Comparing with the same quarter a year earlier matters because December-to-March movements can make the recovery look stronger or weaker than it is.

Margins tell the same story. Gross margin fell to 57.6% from 59.3%, even as operating margin rose to 18.0%. The higher operating profit therefore does not prove stronger product economics. Cash offers firmer support: operating cash rose to $1,534 million from $1,338 million, while free cash flow reached $1,265 million from $1,090 million.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Danaher’s next results?

paragraphs.text: The decisive evidence will be whether underlying demand becomes sales and cash while Masimo’s risks remain contained. Danaher discusses third-quarter results on October 21, 2026, at 8 a.m. Eastern. Julie Sawyer Montgomery became CEO on October 1, so the meeting will show whether she maintains July’s commitments. Investors should look for non-respiratory growth and confirmation of a mid-single-digit exit rate.
